Page 3 Magazine Contact details: Email contributions by the 12th of the month to: contributions.shepleysmag@hotmail.com Write to us and place your letter in the Shepley Magazine Box in the library. All other enquiries including advertising to: shepleysmag@gmail.com If you would like a PDF digital copy of the magazine email: shepleysmag@gmail.com Magazine donations to: Lloyd’s Bank - [bank details in printed issue] or write a cheque out to Shepley’s Magazine and place it in the Shepley Magazine Box in the library, thank you. © Copyright Shepley’s Magazine Welcome to September’s edition Here in Shepley, we are very lucky to have so many people volunteering to make life better for our local residents. We’ve mentioned it before, but it really is a life affirming thing to give up your free time to improve the lives of other people. Perhaps if you’re retired and feeling at a bit of a loose end, volunteering could be just the thing to lift your spirits whilst also supporting the village. In this issue you’ll find several opportunities to join groups as a volunteer. Please have a look through the various articles and see if you would like to get involved. Even this magazine is looking for extra people to help with deliveries, so you could help the community whilst getting fit at the same time! There are a couple of local events this month that are heavily reliant on volunteers. One is Art at the House at Cliffe House on Saturday 19th and Sunday 20th. This is a hugely popular free event with something for all the family. You’ll find entertainment, food, a woodland market, various displays and of course the chance to admire and buy original pieces of artwork. Have a look at the poster in this month’s issue for full details. There are no admission charges and parking is available, but if you live in the village, walking is the best option. Another free village event is the Shepley Over The Years exhibition at St Paul’s Church Hall on Saturday 12th and Sunday 13th, from 2pm. This is part of Heritage Open Days which is a nationwide event run every September to celebrate England’s heritage and culture. It’s run by volunteers and full details can be found on their website: https://www.heritageopendays.org.uk/about-us/press.html Raising money for charity is another positive option for benefitting society. We are very lucky, in this country, to have so many people who will give up their time freely to help charities. In this month’s issue we have the final instalment of local man, Shaun Casey’s run from John o’ Groats to Land’s End raising money for Marie Curie and in the letters page news of another local man, Dave Chew, who is raising money for The Alzheimer’s Society. Very well done to them both. Page 4 When I left Carlisle and wrote the last article, I still had a long way to go. The first part of the journey had taken us from John o’ Groats through some of the most remote and spectacular parts of Scotland, but from Carlisle onwards the landscape, the challenges and the weather changed considerably. I was also now on my own, as Grant had gone home to recover from his injury. From Carlisle I headed south along the Cumbrian Way through the Lake District to Coniston Water, then on to Preston, Southport and Liverpool before crossing into Wales. I followed Offa’s Dyke through Wales before crossing the Severn Bridge and eventually joining the South West Coast Path. I then made my way through Somerset, Devon and Cornwall. There were many fantastic days, and there were also some days when my feet hurt and the miles seemed to go on forever. But the people I met along the way continued to be incredibly generous, kind and supportive. They bought me drinks and meals, let me camp in their gardens and stopped in their droves to have a chat and ask what I was doing. Donations continued to come in from complete strangers I met along the way, friends back home and people who had found my blog and simply wanted to support me. Every donation, whether from someone I knew or someone I had only just met, gave me a real lift and helped make the challenge feel like something bigger than just me running from one end of the country to the other. A huge thank you to everyone who sponsored me, supported me, followed the journey or simply stopped for a chat. And a special thank you to those in Shepley who donated to the challenge. Your support was very much appreciated. To get from John o’ Groats to Land’s End, in 48 days, I took more than 2.3 million steps, ran (and walked) a total of 1,192 miles, climbed the equivalent of 4.5 times the height of Everest and raised £12,410 including Gift Aid. Grant also completed the challenge. When he recovered two weeks later, he went back to Carlisle with his bike and rode down to Land’s End, completing his journey a week before I finished mine. So, we did what we set out to do, and both did Britain End to End. If you would like to contribute to Marie Curie, the link is: justgiving.com/page/britainendtoend Shaun Casey Shaun Casey From Carlisle to Land’s End

Page 6 I first came across Mr Senior of Denby Dale in the mid 1960s when he taught an evening class held in Shepley First School. In those days there were many classes and interest groups to choose from meeting in various venues in local villages. Mr Senior’s subject was ‘Local History’. He was so enthusiastic, interesting and inspiring that his classes were soon oversubscribed. He also led many trips to local historical buildings and churches where he would point out things of special interest. We occasionally went as far as the Yorkshire Dales. Many years later when I retired, I discovered he was still passing on his knowledge at meetings in Shepley Methodist Church. He had established the ‘Yorkshire Studies Group’ in 1997: “To promote interest in the history and heritage of our district and the great county of Yorkshire”. Robert Carter of Kirkburton supported him in his talks and accompanied Mr Senior to Buckingham Palace to receive his MBE award for his unwavering services to local history. When Mr Senior died at the age of 95 in 2000, Robert Carter continued to run the group until his own health failed. Since there was much enthusiasm for the group to continue it was taken on by Pauline Taylor and Dinah Bentley from 2014 to 2025. There is still plenty of interest in the group which is now run by Edward Willis, Martin Whitbread and Lesley Furniss. The first meeting for the autumn term will be 1st October at 2.00pm at Shepley Methodist Church. New and established members will be very welcome and you may pay on the door. Angela Tolson The W.H.Senior MBE Yorkshire Studies Group The origins of the group Mr W. H. Senior Mr Robert Carter

Page 7 Our July members’ meeting saw us sampling the products brought in by Neal’s Yard Remedies representative Tee, who provided lots of information about the benefits of herbal and aromatherapy products. We had good fun doing the ‘sniff tests’ to see if we could distinguish, for example, geranium from rosemary and other scents. We were all surprised at the pleasant scent of patchouli - very different from how most of us remembered it from the 1970s! Both walking groups enjoyed lovely sunshine at their last outings. Our Striders, accompanied by Enzo the dog, explored the moors above Hade Edge, with views across Winscar, Harden and Snailsden reservoirs. Afterwards we had coffee at Totties Garden Centre at Scholes (once we had navigated the closed roads and diversion!) Meanwhile, our Strollers explored the nooks and crannies of Shepley village, followed by a delicious and excellent value for money lunch at Paula’s Community Café in St Paul’s Hall. Also outdoors, the Gardening Group has been busy helping to clear the border outside Shepley Library, as well as sharing their successes and failures in this summer’s drought. The Crafts and Crumbs group continues to meet on the fourth Monday of the month, alongside the café regulars at Shepley Methodist Church. Recently, members have been focusing on their own projects, but no doubt, as we move into autumn (and, dare I say it, edge ever closer to Christmas!), we’ll be experimenting with ideas for seasonal gifts and decorations. Book Club members also met during the summer break to share their holiday reading. Our next members’ meeting is at 7:30pm on Wednesday 16th September, when our speaker will be Paul Jefferies on the subject of ‘Sustainable Tea and Coffee’. Debra Shepley Women’s Institute Our groups continued over the summer

Page 8 Nature seemed to take a break these last few weeks. Apart from hedgerow flowers and of course, butterflies, our outings were characterised by blazing sun and arid landscapes. Josie and Dorothy led a gentle walk from Wooldale, enjoying views from the Cliff to Holme Moss Mast, Castle Hill and the distant Pennines. Totties Garden Centre Café proved irresistible for a coffee break! However, Kath's projected visit to Underbank Reservoir was abandoned because of the excessive heat. Walks have occasionally been postponed or even cancelled due to pouring rain but not heat! Royd Moor Reservoir Nine naturalists enjoyed a delightful 2½ mile stroll around Royd Moor Reservoir. The hedgerows and meadows were bursting with wildflowers, including Common Milk Peas, Vetches, Pink Campions, Sneezeworts and delicate Harebells. Wildlife was abundant: a graceful heron stood quietly by the water's edge while mallards with their ducklings paddled by. Swallows swooped low across the water to feed. Butterflies were no strangers, Cabbage Whites, Peacocks and Gatekeepers were seen fluttering among the bankside flowers. Margaret Lucas Digley-Holme round The walk around Digley Reservoir was on a late July day. It is popular with people and a favourite of ours too. Not one of the hottest days but warm enough to make rucksacks feel heavy and clothes excessive. The heat was perhaps the cause of an absence of birds; Digley Reservoir has never attracted more than a few species of waterbirds, although a family of dabchicks and mallards had been busy a few days before our visit. As for waders, although Curlew are often heard nearby and tiny Common Sandpiper regularly feed along the shore, it is the striking groups of Oyster-Catchers that gather and breed along the embankment; and the woods are usually alive with birdsong, but not today. A large hairy caterpillar, perhaps a "woolly bear", crossed our path leading to tales of sightings of real bears, but sadly nowhere in West Yorkshire. Yellow Rattle was still out in abundance, more brown now than yellow, but still clear evidence of fields that have been traditionally managed. Coming back down through the hayfields, known in earlier times as the Shays, towards the embankment, we spotted two pairs of ears in the field below us - hares in their forms? Or rabbits perhaps? As we swapped opinions they suddenly stood to their full height and raced off down towards the wall, reappearing at the gateway leading to the ever-present herd of highland cattle. Hares, then! Back to the cars finally seeing an oystercatcher rising up loudly from the embankment; we also saw swooping martins and swallows, then the rare sight of a large group of lapwings splashing and preening on the stony edge in preparation for their coming flight away from their breeding grounds; and over them all a buzzard floating languidly above. Pauline Taylor and David Fisher Silkstone Walk and Lunch These occasional but regular walks culminating in a pub meal always manage to attract a considerable number of members. Sue has found a winning formula where half of us opt to walk and the other half head straight for the pub! Rodger led us through the attractive and historic village of Silkstone, pausing to read the poignant account of the Huskar Pit disaster of 1838 carved on a substantial monument in the churchyard. Twenty- six children aged between 7 and 17 were drowned in the flooded mine. Reaching the track bed of the former wagonway we followed it through the woods and ambled back up to the Bells (formerly Ring o' Bells) where we were welcomed with an excellent meal and cooling drinks. Page 9 Did you know that our resident population of Robins, that traditional bird of the Christmas card, will be joined by Robins from Europe, Scandinavia and Russia, all finding our climate easier to endure before flying back home in the spring? If you’re looking forward to the cooler days ahead, then we have some wonderful suggestions for warm and entertaining evenings close to home in Cliffe House with our new programme of talks. All these are designed to be of interest to beginners and the more experienced and our speakers are happy to answer any and all questions. By venturing outside with us on our field visits, we hope to increase your love and understanding of birds and wildlife. Discover how any winter blues can be blown away in an instant with sightings of migrant birds arriving to enjoy our warmer winter climate and sharing that experience with others. Shepley Bird and Wildlife Group That friendly Robin may be Russian! Contacts details: email: shepleybirders@yahoo.com Tel: Chris Marks 01484 608652 Our indoor meetings start on Wednesday September 2nd at 7.30pm, Cliffe House, Coach House when Ray Brown the local wildlife photographer will be telling us more about his favourite studies of birds and animals. To attend as a visitor there is a charge of £3.00. Field visits are free so just let us know if you’d like to join us and we can promise fresh air and a great deal of good humour. Feel free to pick and mix any of the talks or field visits or join the group for the modest fee of £15 per year. Details of all our talks will be available in these monthly magazine articles and programmes from your local libraries or by request using the contact details below. We look forward to welcoming you. Page 15 YORKSHIRE DAY (officially August 1st) came into being initially in 1975 as a protest against some in local government who were wanting to mess with the county's boundaries. It seemed that their protest was successful and from then on Yorkshire Day has been celebrated around the county in lots of places with the events taking many different forms. Shepley Methodist Church decided to have a fun celebration of Yorkshire Day this year on the nearest Sunday which was August 2nd and everyone was invited. The church was decorated with the white rose of Yorkshire flag and bunting and even a few balloons with a sheep logo on them and the celebration comprised of poems, a light-hearted quiz and songs, and even our bible reading (taken from the Yorkshire Passport!) was spoken in the Yorkshire dialect. The children coloured in a picture of a Yorkshire man with his flat cap and completed a wordsearch too. Highlights were the ‘Ode to the Emley Tower’ written and presented by Maggie (see last month's magazine) and Rita singing ‘Scarborough Fair’. There was lots of laughter, and we even recalled the founder of Methodism, John Wesley’s experience in the county when he wrote in his diary, "I rode over the mountains to Huddersfield. A wilder people I never saw in England. The men, women and children filled the streets as we rode along and seemed ready to devour us" and then when visiting nearby Barnsley, he said, "I turned aside to Barnsley famous for all manner of wickedness," so not such a good write up from Mr Wesley. We did acknowledge the painful times endured by many in our county during and for many years after the Industrial Revolution when workers flocked to the towns in search of work and lived in appalling conditions. This was summed up in the Dalesman’s Litany. Our celebration continued afterwards when there were buns made to the famous Fat Rascal recipe, Yorkshire ginger cake and buttered scones for everyone, all washed down with a cup of Yorkshire tea. It was good fun and a great joy to celebrate our County of Yorkshire as a part of God's creation. We have two celebrations coming up soon at Shepley Methodist Church. The first is our HARVEST FESTIVAL on Sunday 11th October led by Church Minister, Revd Sue and then secondly our CHURCH ANNIVERSARY on 25th October, led by preacher Kimm Brooke. There is also a service for REMEMBRANCE SUNDAY, 8th November, led by Revd Sue, you might like to pop into your diary. Everyone is welcome to all the services and of course any Sunday morning at Shepley Methodist Church when we start at 10.45am. It would be lovely to see you. Contact: Revd Sue Pegg – 07931 832456 Shepley Methodist Church A fun celebration of Yorkshire Day

Page 16 Yew Tree Road is marked on the early maps of Shepley and literally led to woodland rich in yew trees. Linking Station Road to the old toll road (Abbey Road) it has a brook flowing through the bottom which is still visible at some points. In 1859 a tenant farmer was prosecuted because chemicals from his dye house had killed all the fish downstream. At the top of the hill near Station Road is a farmhouse built in 1685 by Edward Walker. His initials are still over the door. Originally a laith house, where the occupants lived on one side and the animals on the other, the property has since been divided into two homes. Most of the houses actually bordering the road are fairly modern, but there are older rows of cottages, commonly known as the Co-op rows as they were built by the Shepley Co-operative Society. The top row was constructed in the 1920s and the bottom row in the 1930s. As the road rises towards the main road there was once a market garden containing numerous greenhouses called Rillside. This was run by Albert Kaye. He had a wooden greengrocer’s shop nearby, where he sold his produce. He would often be working in the garden so if customers called, they used a bell to summon him. The shop tended to get busy at weekends and Roger Smith remembered watching the queues from his home as a boy, then dashing across the field to make his purchases when it got quieter. Other residents included George and Turner Woodhead and Willie Payne, all cattle dealers. Clare Francis With thanks to Norman Smith and David Billington’s team (who completed and shared much of this thorough research). A snapshot of Shepley’s history Yew Tree Road

Page 17 We had a lovely day at the invitation of OurCoop to attend the New Mill Community Fun Day. This is a yearly event where OurCoop brings families together over the summer holidays. The Membership & Community Council who fund the day provide co-operative education activities to highlight the recreational and educational activities that the Society provides. A number of stall holders attended from Kirklees Council. Riverholme provided educational work from bug houses to identifying different water species in the garden. A Scrap Plastic workshop was offered and other activities included weaving of willow fishes, potato printing and stone painting. The volunteers at the Community Garden also provided the opportunity for the young people to do some potting and learning about the gardens and showcasing this wonderful oasis of beautiful gardens and woodland which was a pleasure for everyone. The event concluded with a free picnic provided by OurCoop with sandwiches, crisps, drinks and cake, which is always a highlight when the food arrives. People then take their time to sit around in the surroundings to enjoy time together as a family. Page 23 Parliament breaks for recess over summer, meaning I get to spend more time in our area. Now I’ve made no secret that I prefer spending time out in our community to being in Westminster (nothing beats a good Yorkshire welcome or a day at a gala!), but it also provides a real chance to have important conversations with people across our towns and villages. One thing that has come up recently has been concerns about increased numbers of vape and betting shops in nearby towns, making their high streets less appealing as they crowd out the shops and services people love and rely on. I’ve spoken often with my colleagues about the need to tackle this issue and I am proud that the Government is putting power back in the hands of local communities to have a real say over what opens on their high street. We are putting in place new planning rules to ensure vape shops and adult gaming centres can’t just pop up without local people having a say and to give councils the power to ban them near schools. I will work with Kirklees Council to make sure they use these powers to rebuild pride in towns near us. I also met with SCARD, an amazing local organisation that supports families who have lost loved ones in road traffic accidents. They provide 1-1 support and counselling for as long as the person needs it, being there when people need it most. SCARD is run by people with such compassion and care, and I am proud to support them in their work. I also had the real privilege to open Shelley Gala at the Cricket Club. It’s such an amazing event, bringing together our community for over 90 years! Events like this can only happen with the hard work of volunteers. With help all the way from Shelley's Over 60s Club down to the children at Shelley First School, it was a real testament to the entire community, and I was so happy to be there. The work the Government and I are doing originates from conversations I’ve had with local people, so as ever, do reach out to me and my team. John Taylor, our Kirklees Councillor, is currently unwell and unable to write his regular monthly report for Shepley Magazine. He sends his apologies to everyone and hopes to be back as soon as he can. John is having treatment for a kidney infection and we all wish him a speedy recovery. Dinah Bentley Shepley Health Centre Five things patients can do 1. Ask questions If you are unsure about your diagnosis, treatment or care plan, ask your healthcare team to explain. 2. Know your medicines Keep an up-to-date list of your medicines and understand what each one is for and how to take it. 3. Check your information Make sure important details—such as your name, medicines, allergies and medical history—are correct. 4. Understand what happens next Before leaving an appointment or hospital, make sure you know what follow-up care, tests or appointments are needed. 5. Speak up If something doesn't seem right or you are worried about your care, tell a member of your healthcare team. Your concerns matter. Shepley Evergreens Tea Committee receipts from1959

However, the many routine visits to Leeds and the long waits in crowded corridors have been less than welcome, so I was really delighted to discover that the Kirburton Eye Care Practice could offer me the same remedial treatment. I cannot recommend this practice highly enough; we are so fortunate to have them so near to where we live. Page 30 Around the Club As summer begins to wind down, so too does another busy cricket season at Shepley. It takes a huge effort from our volunteers and ground staff to keep pace with the constant activity — especially during the peak weeks when cup fixtures stack on top of already full league schedules. That effort continues to be one of our greatest strengths, and we remain incredibly proud of the amount of cricket we are able to facilitate at Marsh Lane. This month we are shining a spotlight on the fantastic progress made across our Women’s and Girls’ sections. With a few fixtures still to come for the Senior Men’s and the odd junior game, a full round up of the season for those teams follows in the next edition. Fundraising Back in May, we set an ambitious fundraising target of £31,000 to support the development of a new all-weather nursery ground. This project will allow us to expand opportunities for Women’s, Girls’ and Junior cricket, easing pressure on our main square which is already stretched to capacity. Thanks to the generosity of the local community — and a significant contribution from Sport England (The National Lottery) — we are well on our way to making this vision a reality. Once the season ends, we hope to quickly see the ground being developed in the hope that the new pitch will be up and running for the 2027 season! Women’s Cricket After entering just one softball team in 2025, we took a huge step forward this year with one hardball team and two softball teams competing in 2026. That leap has transformed our programme: the number of games played has risen dramatically, and with league standings at stake, the cricket has been far more competitive. In our first ever season of Women’s Hardball Cricket, the team currently sits 2nd in the league. Although our fixtures are complete, a couple of other results could see us finish 3rd — but either way, ending the season in the top three is an outstanding achievement. Our Women’s 1st Softball team enjoyed a perfect campaign, finishing top of the league with eight wins from eight. The Women’s 2nd Softball team also impressed, finishing 2nd, winning seven of their nine matches. Across the summer, our women’s teams played 30 games, with 24 women representing the club — a breakthrough season in every sense. A huge well done to all players, organisers, coaches and umpires who made it possible. Shepley Cricket Club Spotlight on Women’s and Girls’ cricket

Page 31 Girls’ Cricket This year we entered teams into both the U11 and U13 Girls’ leagues. The U13 Girls spent most of the season near the top of the table, narrowly missing out on the title after a close defeat to Thongsbridge CC in the penultimate game. Their batting and bowling were consistently excellent, but it was the teams fielding and teamwork that truly stood out — something regularly praised by opposition coaches as well as our own. For the U11 Girls, the focus is on festival-style cricket with round-robin formats. Results matter far less at this age; it’s all about participation, enjoyment and learning the game. The girls embraced every opportunity brilliantly. Any girls in the village who want to get involved please let us know. The number of girls participating at cricket, either girls only or mixed, has increased massively in recent years. We now offer cricket for girls from aged 5 through to senior women’s cricket and everything in between – softball, and a little bit of hardball if you are feeling brave! Until next month…when hopefully I can summarise the season for all the other teams, maybe even some good news with the 2nd Team currently sitting top of the league…fingers crossed.
